# Looking at Things {#chp:printing}

Printing is where you find out whether your object is what you think it is.
The base R printers are fine, but they often add quotes, indices, and escape
sequences that get in the way. This chapter covers recipes that show you the
content as it really is, and a few that draw structure you can scan at a
glance.

## Print text {#sec:grp-print-text}

Strings and files, shown without quotes and indices.

### Print strings without the noise {#sec:raw-string}

Printing a character vector shows indices, quotes, and escape sequences. That is
useful for debugging, but not when you want to see the text itself. `raw_string()`
drops all of that:

```{r}
x = c("line one", "say \"hello\"", "tab\there")
x            # with indices and escapes
raw_string(x)  # what the strings actually contain
```

### Read a text file into the console {#sec:file-string}

`file_string()` reads a whole file into one string and prints it cleanly as a
side effect. Pass `comment = ''` to the chunk and the output looks like the file
itself:

```{r comment=''}
f = system.file("LICENSE", package = "xfun")
file_string(f)
```

## Display objects {#sec:grp-display}

Structure and sizes, laid out so you can scan them.

### Draw the shape of a nested object {#sec:tree}

Nested lists are hard to read through `str()`, since the depth markers `..`
all look alike. `tree()` redraws `str()` output as a tree, with vertical pipes
connecting parents and children:

```{r}
fit = lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
tree(fit)
```

### Show a list as tabs {#sec:tabset}

When a list is too big to print in one go, put each member in its own tab.
`tabset()` turns a list into Markdown tabsets, one tab per member. Nested lists
become nested tabsets. By default each tab shows `str()` output, but you can
pass any function you like:

```{r}
survey = list(
  meta = list(date = '2026-11-07', n = 6),
  scores = list(
    math = c(90, 85, 72, 64, 98, 80),
    reading = c(70, 95, 88, 91, 60, 77)
  ),
  notes = 'Two students retook the reading test.'
)
tabset(survey)
```

The top level has three tabs, and `meta` and `scores` each hold a nested set of
tabs. Pass a
function to change what each tab shows, such as a numeric summary instead of
`str()`. If the function returns `tab_content()`, the Markdown you give it is
used as the tab content as is:

```{r}
tabset(survey, function(x) {
  if (is.numeric(x) && length(x) > 1) print(summary(x))
  else tab_content(paste('**Value:**', x))
})
```

Inside a **litedown** document, the CSS and JS that the tabs need are added for
you. You don't have to enable them in the document metadata.

### Make file sizes readable {#sec:format-bytes}

Raw byte counts are hard to scan. `format_bytes()` turns them into strings with
sensible units:

```{r}
format_bytes(c(500, 2048, 1.5e6, 3e9))
```
